items.title: Looking for a summer job? Here’s what to consider
paras: There's an influx of hospitality, retail and tourism jobs over summer, economist Blair Chapman says. ( ABC News: Sam Ikin )
If you're looking for a few extra hours of work or desperately trying to save before university begins, a summer job could be the right fit for you.
These seasonal roles can simply be about earning extra cash, but it could help you discover what you love (or hate) doing for work.
Ben Walker was 16 when he got a casual job at his local supermarket in Sale, in regional Victoria.
Ben Walker's first casual job led to ongoing part-time work. ( Supplied: Ben Walker )
The 21-year-old says that led to the part-time job that now supports him while studying game design at university.
In the beginning, Ben says he learnt a lot from interactions with people outside of school and cricket.
There is an influx of roles in hospitality, retail and tourism ahead of Christmas and summer, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at employment service Seek.
"In Australia we get the double dose of Christmas and summer," he says.
Retail picks up from early November (because of Black Friday sales), and online shopping has led to an increase in warehouse or "pick-packer roles" too, Dr Chapman says.
And given cost-of-living pressures and airfare prices, more Australians are likely to holiday closer to home this summer, he says.
"That sort of domestic-driven tourism might pick up because people can't afford to go overseas."
Dr Chapman says there is also "a bit of an evolution" in who is looking for summer jobs.
"There's a cost-of-living crunch and people are looking for that second job to help supplement their income," he says.
Grozdana Manalo says her first job as a barista began a "love affair" with coffee and helped her build confidence and communication skills.
"It also showed me just how hard and long some people work and made me really appreciate being a uni student," she says.
She's now a career services manager at the University of Sydney's Business School.
"Summer jobs can also help students discover what they enjoy, and just as importantly, what they don't," Ms Manalo says.
Seasonal and casual roles can also help young people develop professional skills, she says.
"Teamwork, communication, problem solving and time management — all important skills no matter what job or career you pick in the future."
Irma Mooi-Reci is a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the CEO of a company specialising in workforce data and skill gaps.
She would like young people to think "more strategically" about summer employment.
"Is it because you want to pay your bills? Is it because you want to have that experience or get a reference? Or is it because you want to get that first permanent job?" she asks.
It's worth looking for a job that complements your career goals and whether an employer will see the experience as relevant, Professor Mooi-Reci says.
"Find something that you like doing, that you feel passionate about and learn as much as possible."
Professor Mooi-Reci says young people can become overwhelmed by information and fearmongering about the job market, the value of their degree and artificial intelligence.
If you're after seasonal work, Ms Manalo recommends looking for roles advertised on social media and job boards, or simply walking into local businesses and asking if there are positions available.
She says there are also "hidden job markets", which is why so many positions are filled before they're advertised.
"This is all about leveraging your personal networks and making it known that you're looking for work," she says.
If you're young or have never been employed before, understanding workplace rights and responsibilities is very important, Ms Manalo says.
But Professor Mooi-Reci says it can be tricky for some people to resist jobs that have low pay and poor conditions.
Avoid jobs that seem exploitative and look for other options, she adds.
Ms Manalo says it's also important to keep records of the hours you've worked.
"Review your pay slips, and ask questions if something doesn't seem right," she says.
She recommends the Fair Work Ombudsman website for information and assistance regarding your rights and entitlements.

items.title: Data centres driving up inflation and community concerns
paras: Signs litter properties near Firmus's proposed AI data centre site in Prospect Vale, northern Tasmania. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid )
But right now they're doing much more: they're at the centre of concern about how much their construction is stoking inflation.
And, they're a lightning rod for communities rising up against what they feel is the cost of rapid growth.
" Over the last year, we've obviously seen an absolute explosion in our pipeline," IBISWorld research analyst Andrew Ledovskikh says.
His research has found Australia currently has about 2.3 gigawatts (GW) worth of power capacity in 79 data centres.
That's enough to power about 1.5 million homes, depending how you work the numbers.
Planned projects would give Australia capacity estimated to be more than 10 times that — between 23 and 67GW — according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.
Not all projects make it, and Commonwealth Bank research forecasts 9GW of capacity by 2035.
Data centre capacity is expected to grow rapidly. ( Supplied: AEMO/CBA )
"We really are just at the beginning. This is the moment where the water sort of recedes back into the beach and everything's calm before the tsunami hits," Mr Ledovskikh said.
For advocates such as Belinda Dennett, it's an "enormous opportunity", with a construction timeline supporting our economy.
Belinda Dennett believes building data centres can help transform Australia's economy. ( ABC News: Jack Ailwood )
Lamenting that "we've missed other global technology waves", Ms Dennett said this boom was a chance to "build on our advantages in cheap renewable energy".
"We can transform our economy and ensure Australia's future prosperity."
For opponents such as Judy Gunson, however, the mushrooming sites are an "invasion" of neighbourhoods.
In recent years, data centres have become a magnet for controversy in Europe and the US over the impact of noise, light and sheer size of the centres on neighbouring properties.
Then there are environmental and economic concerns, because they use, and drive up, the cost of water and power.
US-based political scientist David McCuan has seen this issue take off, and quickly.
An expert in political science at Sonoma State University, Professor McCuan said the backlash to the rapid growth of the centres meant there was "bipartisan" opposition in recent elections.
Anti-data centre demonstrators have had significant success in the US. ( AP: Marc Levy )
Anti-data centre measures were on the ballot in more than 40 different jurisdictions in the midterms.
A temporary ban, called a moratorium, is in place in New York and Texas has paused connections to the electricity grid — effectively stopping development.
" The battle that we see going on over data centres and AI, that unites both [political] sides," Professor McCuan said.

"They've affected a governor's race in Texas, they've affected local issues in zoning for what's going on in Ohio or in the Midwest. That's not something we would have forecast, say, eight, 10, 12 months ago."
"The potential to derail any slow progress we're making towards reducing [carbon] emissions by this rollout, which is using extraordinary amounts of power."
We're standing in the shadow of the Westgate Bridge, next to Melbourne's busy container port.
What used to be the printing plant for the Herald Sun newspaper is being cleared for a massive data centre, to be built by NEXTDC.
Judy Gunson is a spokeswoman for the Port Melbourne data centre action group. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley )
The community activist is protesting the build, concerned about the speedy pace and enormous scale of data centre construction.
Communities in Sydney and Launceston are just some of those that have objected to development of the centres.
A dispute about power poles hit plans for the expansion of an existing NEXTDC site in the inner-west of Melbourne.
The fight wiped $3 billion off the listed company's value when the share price cratered 42 per cent in one day. The share price recovered after a rival company bought up a huge amount, cheaply.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is currently attempting to "cool" the Australian economy by lifting interest rates.
The aim is to lower the speed of prices rising, a force called inflation. Consumer prices are going up by 4.3 per cent annually at the moment.

Along with rocketing fuel prices due to war in the Middle East, the rapid construction of data centres and spending on artificial intelligence (AI) is often slated for overheating our economy and driving up inflation.
An internal RBA note suggests local data centre operators have raised record capital of at least $35 billion so far this year, fuelling rapid construction of AI infrastructure.
That's 46 per cent more than the 2025 figure, and even the central bank thinks it is a conservative guess.
Michele Bullock believes data centre technology is not currently putting pressure on the country's economy. ( AAP: Dan Himbrechts )

In a press conference after the most recent rate hike , RBA governor Michele Bullock said a huge proportion, "maybe 70 per cent", of data centre technology was imported, so was "not putting pressure on the Australian economy and Australian goods and services".
Where it does, she said, is in pushing up prices for scarce construction materials and skilled labourers.
"There is a chunk and it's related to building the warehouses and getting electricians to come in and install the servers and all those sorts of things.
"That does put pressure on Australian resources, and that's where it might be putting inflationary pressure in."
Ms Bullock said the hope was that, over time, data centre investment would lead to gains in productivity, which would ultimately lower inflation.
For a long time, data centres looked like warehouses and were set in industrial areas.
The hyper-scale push means they're growing far larger and are increasingly encroaching on residential and farming land, which brings developers into conflict with the communities around them .

The Victorian government went into a caretaker period ahead of this month's election, before Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny made a decision on nine contentious data centre projects that had been "fast-tracked" to her office.
A statement from a Labor spokesperson, after the deadline, said all proposals went through a "rigorous planning process":
The spokesperson pointed to a policy that required new developments to source their own renewable power and not be near schools.

items.title: The cost of basics keeps rising but 'anti-fascist economics' could lower them
paras: Isabella Weber, an associate professor of economics, says the soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies.
In a new book, she says policymakers need to make affordability the centre of "anti-fascist economics".
Dr Weber says it will require "structuralist measures" that change the ways in which we provision the essentials in society.
Isabella Weber, a rising-star German economist, says it is something we need to pursue again.
She says fascism has made a comeback. Our economic and political systems have stopped making our lives better and people are furious about it.

She says illiberal forces are exploiting voters' anger and, rather than addressing the material causes of their pain, are deliberately redirecting people's rage towards migrants and other minorities, and promising that salvation can be found in nationalism, ethnic purity or patriarchy.

To combat the phenomenon, she argues, we have to make life's essentials affordable again — housing, food, energy, water, health care, transport — so the foundations for a dignified life are available to everyone, no matter your household income or class.
"It's funny that today we think of anti-fascist economics as provocative," she told the ABC Business Daily podcast .
"In the 1940s it was actually a mainstream point for economists to say that economics had a role to play in 'Never Again'.
"I would argue that today we are [once again] in a deep crisis of democracy around the Western world. The extreme right is on the rise. Democracy is as unstable as it has been since the 40s.
"I think people are very clear. They're saying they can't take the status quo anymore," she said.
Isabella Weber speaks to the ABC about her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. ( ABC News )
Dr Weber, an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, shot to prominence (or notoriety) in December 2021.

She published an op-ed in The Guardian arguing that, in the wake of the COVID lockdowns, it could be worth using temporary and strategic price controls on certain products to prevent large companies in systemically significant sectors from exploiting the chaos to make windfall profits (and sending higher prices through the system).

She said they were a standard tool of economic management in the 1940s. They had been used to prevent inflation spiking dangerously in the transitional years when warfare economies were shifting back from a supply-constrained world with pent-up consumer demand (and high household savings) to post-war peacetime economies when domestic supply had recovered.
She saw strong parallels between the two historical periods. But the fallout from her article was immediate.

"In a matter of hours, Weber, who was 33 years old, had transformed from an obscure but respected academic … into the most hated woman in economics — simply for proposing a 'serious conversation about strategic price controls'," Zach Carter wrote in The New Yorker .
Weber agrees that her article "touched a nerve deep inside the economics establishment".
"The idea that targeted price controls as an emergency measure merit serious consideration was greeted as if I had recommended a pornography exhibition in the Vatican," she writes in her book.

"[But] for months, in public earnings calls with their shareholders, corporate leaders had been gleefully celebrating the fact that the pandemic, spiking commodity prices, and supply chain dislocations provided a wonderful opportunity to jack up prices.

"As my co-authors and I later showed with research powered by large-language models analysing 138,962 earnings calls, corporate leaders tend to talk positively about generalised cost shocks, which impact workers and households negatively, because they are good for pricing and the bottom line."
Jump forward to 2026, and Weber says the high inflation that so many countries are still experiencing is one big problem among many.

She says it is adding to the pressure-cooker environment that millions of people have been living in for decades, where the costs of basic essentials such as housing, food, energy and health have been rising much faster than prices of non-essentials such as TVs, electronics and toys.
The graphic below shows what happened to the price of essentials and non-essentials in the United States between 2000 and 2022. When it was published a few years ago it went viral on the internet.
( Supplied: Nick Routley, Visual Capitalist, Consumer price inflation, by type of good or service (2000-2022), February 22, 2023 )
It illuminates a point Dr Weber is making about the drivers of inequality under neoliberal capitalism.
She says when people living in the richest countries in the world are still struggling to pay for basics it is unsurprising they are so angry.

In her book, she argues that modern scarcities in basic public services and housing are the outgrowth of decades of austerity and "market subordination at all costs" and that that scarcity has become "the breeding ground of hate".
"Price shocks in essentials are always simultaneously inequality shocks," she writes.
"Usually we only consider income dynamics like wage stagnation as the driver of inequality increases … [but] price increases in essentials can be of similar importance."
In the book, she explains that anti-fascist economics is not her idea. It used to be commonplace.
Karl Polanyi, the Austrian émigré scholar who theorised about fascism in the 1930s and 1940s (and from which he had to flee to London) was one economist who wrote about it in detail.

She told the ABC that "anti-fascist economics" would improve peoples' lives, and rebuild their faith in democracy, by securing and delivering the necessities for people at affordable prices and with their affordability safeguarded.

Dr Weber says we have levels of corporate concentration today, including in essential sectors, where a handful of companies have control over the things that people and industry can not do without, and that is a problem that needs addressing.
"In the 1940s [it] actually was one of the arguments that economists made that, you know, whoever controls the essentials has quite a considerable degree of control over [an] economy and society.
"And as such, in a democracy, we have to ask the question of how we organise the essentials."
"But it's also a question of, you know, whose interests are political representatives actually standing up for?

"Under neoliberalism, we have been telling people for decades that democracy is the greatest of all political systems, which of course it is, but at the same time, even when it comes to the most basic things you need for a dignified life, 'There's not much that the elected representatives can do for you.'

"Anti-fascist economics is about creating an economic policy playbook that addresses the essentials, makes them affordable with short-run measures, and then introduces more structuralist measures that change the ways in which we provision the essentials."

items.title: ASX dips lower, Nvidia scandal weighs on Wall Street
paras: Advertisement Updated Business Markets World markets ASX dips lower, Nvidia scandal weighs on Wall Street Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated November 16, 2026 — 10:12am , first published 5:21am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
Share A A A The Australian sharemarket has opened lower after US stocks fell on Friday to cap off a turbulent week on Wall Street.
The S&P/ASX 200 was down 6.5 points to 9075.7 in early trade on Monday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US67.92¢.

In New York, the S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent on Friday, but managed to post a 2.5 per cent gain for the week. This marks the benchmark index’s first winning week since October and its biggest weekly gain since August.

The volatility around Nvidia kept Wall Street on its toes on Friday. Bloomberg The Dow Jones Industrial Average recovered from an early slide and eked out a 0.1 per cent gain. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.9 per cent, but also notched its first weekly gain in five weeks.

The major indexes have been shaky this week as some of the biggest AI companies pushed and pulled the market. Many of those companies have big stock values with a heavier impact on the market’s gains or losses.

The market remained unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The company has been the face of the AI industry, which has been responsible for much of the gains, and big swings, on Wall Street.

Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised US national security concerns. Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO. The ensuing fallout cost Nvidia’s market cap just under $US600 billion ($883 billion) this week.

The AI industry’s influence over Wall Street was evident again Friday, as the slump in technology stocks with a big focus on AI weighed on the market, even though more than 60 per cent of the stocks within the S&P 500 rose.

Nvidia was again among the heaviest weights and it fell 2 per cent. Broadcom fell 4.8 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 8.8 per cent. Both companies saw their shares surge earlier this week as the management shake-up at Nvidia unfolded.

Nvidia in particular has been slipping for weeks amid wider concerns about a potential slowdown for the industry. The big worry has been whether AI will produce enough profit to justify the costly investments and big stock values.

“Nvidia’s pullback serves as a reminder of the concentration risk embedded in a market where a small number of mega-cap technology stocks have driven an outsized share of returns,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.
Outside of AI, Microsoft rose 0.2 per cent, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications.
Among the gainers were healthcare and financial stocks. Eli Lilly and Co. rose 1.3 per cent. Payment processors Visa and Mastercard also closed 1.3 per cent higher.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 30.73 points to 7,561.67. The index is up 10.5 per cent so far this year.
The Dow gained 50.46 points to 52,347.55, and the Nasdaq gave up 229.82 points to close at 25,136.27.

Oil prices swung a day after President Donald Trump said that the US didn’t “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It settled at $US95.84 a barrel. It was trading near $US72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.
Treasury yields were mixed in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 5.15 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday.

The yield on the two-year Treasury rose to 4.87 per cent from 4.86 per cent late Thursday. It closely tracks expectations for action from the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting in an effort to cool stubbornly hot inflation.

A report on Friday showed that wholesale inflation cooled a bit last month, but remains very high. The report measures inflation experienced by businesses, before it can reach consumers. Inflation at the consumer level remains stubbornly high at well above 3 per cent. That’s also much higher than the Fed’s preferred target of 2 per cent.

Rising energy prices because of the US war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising.
The latest wholesale inflation report also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.

“That suggests inflation is working its way into the broader economy rather than remaining concentrated in the original areas of price pressure,” said Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, in a research note. “If that continues, it becomes much harder for the Fed to simply look through inflation as temporary.”

The central bank held rates steady at its last meeting, following a previous rate hike. The latest hot updates on inflation have prompted economists to overwhelmingly expect a rate hike at the upcoming December meeting, with another hike likely to follow in January.
Rate hikes by the Fed can cool inflation, but that makes borrowing more expensive and can slow economic growth.

items.title: Police charge 14-year-old boy over crash of allegedly stolen car
paras: A teenage girl is in a critical condition after an allegedly stolen car crashed into another vehicle in Tingalpa on Sunday. ( ABC News )
Police have charged a 14-year-old boy over a two-vehicle crash at Tingalpa, in Brisbane's east.
Three teenage passengers were injured in the incident, with one girl taken to hospital in a critical condition.
The teenage boy will face Brisbane Children's Court charged with a range of offences.
A 14-year-old boy has been charged over a two-vehicle crash in Brisbane's south-east involving an allegedly stolen car that left three other teenagers in hospital.

Emergency services were called to the intersection of Wynnum and Hemmant Tingalpa Roads just before 4pm on Sunday following reports a white Toyota Corolla had collided with another vehicle and crashed into a power pole.
Police allege the white Toyota had been reported stolen from Wynnum earlier in the day.
The alleged driver of the vehicle, a 14-year-old boy and three passengers in the car, two 15-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy, were transported to hospital.
The occupants of the other vehicle were physically uninjured. ( ABC News )
The crash knocked out power for more than 1,200 households in the area for several hours.

The 14-year-old boy has been charged with three counts of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death or grievous bodily harm, enter premises and commit indictable offence, driving of a motor vehicle without a licence and proceeding through a red traffic light.
Police are asking any witnesses or anyone with vision of the incident to come forward.

items.title: Oil, smoke and Myanmar: The key issues facing South-East Asia
paras: Jeepney drivers, a critical part of the Philippines' transportation system, protest the high fuel prices prompted by the war in the Middle East ahead of the ASEAN summit. ( Reuters: Eloisa Lopez )
World leaders are in the Philippines today, engaging in a flurry of high-level diplomacy amid a destabilised global order and rising geopolitical tensions.
This year's Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila will set the tone before US President Donald Trump and other leaders head to China for APEC talks.
A meeting of the Quad is also likely; the strategic partnership between India, Japan, Australia and the United States that is seen as a means of checking China's growing influence across Asia.
With numerous global challenges, these issues are set to dominate the ASEAN agenda.
The war in the Middle East is making it much more expensive to refuel in car-centric Manila. ( Reuters: Eloisa Lopez )
The war in Iran and the ensuing chaos in global energy markets are front of mind for leaders, as much of South-East Asia is heavily reliant on oil and gas from the Middle East.
Hunter Marston, South-East Asia program director at the Lowy Institute, said the energy issue has been "massive".
"It's triggered protests … and has caused enormous headaches for political leaders," he said.
"ASEAN this year has been emphasising progress towards a strategic petroleum reserve and the ASEAN power grid.
"These are both signals of the recognition that ASEAN needs to do something to shore up its regional resilience and its ability to withstand external shocks."
Theresa Lazaro is the Philippines' Secretary of Foreign Affairs. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston )
For decades, ASEAN nations have been investigating ways to connect electricity infrastructure across nations to bolster energy security.
Philippines Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told the ABC that discussions are underway to advance these regional energy resilience projects.
"Of course, it's a very expensive and protracted issue, but I think it's really about time that we have to implement this ASEAN energy grid," she said.
The Philippines has faced repeated incidents over competing territorial claims in the South China Sea. ( AP: Aaron Favila )
While competing territorial claims in the South China Sea have always been a key issue for ASEAN nations, these disputes will hit close to home this year.
The Philippines has experienced numerous maritime confrontations with China over the contested waterway.
China claims almost all of the South China Sea through its "nine-dash line", a claim a tribunal at The Hague found to have no basis under international maritime law a decade ago.
Despite this, China is accused of employing low-level acts of aggression below the threshold of armed conflict, including blasting Philippine Coast Guard vessels and fishing boats with water cannons.
ASEAN has been trying to negotiate a Code of Conduct with China to de-escalate tensions and provide a framework for dealing with disputes.
The Philippines was hopeful it would be finalised by the end of this summit, although that now appears unlikely.
China's claims in the South China Sea cut through the majority of its neighbours' claims. ( ABC News graphic: Jarrod Fankhauser )
Mr Marston wasn't sure if the final code of conduct would reduce tensions or the risk of escalation.
"It's not clear that this will constrain China's behaviour in the South China Sea," he said.
"(But) it has tied ASEAN member states and Beijing together in the process of negotiations."
Mr Marston said the code doesn't hold China "accountable" and China had previously violated the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea despite being one of the first countries to sign up.
Meanwhile, Australia signed a defence agreement with the Philippines this month to further support its coast guard and navy.
Myanmar's military took power following a coup in 2021. ( Reuters: Ann Wang )

More than five years after Myanmar's military junta seized control of the country in a coup, the conflict between the military, pro-democracy resistance groups and ethnic armed organisations continues to rage on.
An estimated 100,000 people have been killed and millions displaced, according to UN officials.
Elections held earlier this year helped junta leader Min Aung Hlaing become president; however, they were widely dismissed by critics as a "sham".
ASEAN adopted a "Five-Point Consensus" shortly after the coup, calling for an end to violence, dialogue, mediation, humanitarian assistance and visits by an envoy.
Despite criticism of the plan's implementation, ASEAN has stuck with it.
Ms Lazaro recently visited Myanmar as an envoy, describing the "situation" as "deplorable".
Aung San Suu Kyi was detained following a coup in 2021. ( Myanmar State TV )
Ms Lazaro didn't meet with former Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi but was told she was "doing well".
The 81-year-old was moved to house arrest earlier this year and was visited by a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Myanmar's leader, Min Aung Hlaing, and high-level junta politicians are barred from ASEAN meetings to pressure the military-backed government to implement the Five-Point Consensus.
But analysts believe some ASEAN countries, which have been re-establishing bilateral ties with Myanmar, have been undermining these efforts.
Ms Lazaro said those countries were "just recalibrating their bilateral relationships" rather than undermining the consensus.
The US has also been holding secretive talks with Myanmar, possibly to gain access to its enormous reserves of rare earth metals, pivotal in the manufacturing of modern technologies.
At this year's summit, discussions are underway between ASEAN nations over whether to end the ban on Myanmar's military-backed leaders attending the meetings.
Motorists on the Kahayan Bridge travel through a haze as wildfires shroud the area. ( Reuters: Usep Hariadi )
A Super El Niño weather pattern is in full swing across South-East Asia, projected to peak in late 2026 and early 2027.
The intensity of the weather phenomenon has brought drought, extreme heat and agricultural disruptions across large parts of the region.
In Indonesia, it has underpinned the worst forest and land fire season in more than a decade, worsening underlying conditions as "slash and burn" fires are lit to clear land for plantations.
The fires have at times blanketed large swathes of Indonesia and travelled across borders, covering Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines in toxic smoke.
The smoke has caused diplomatic tensions between Indonesia and Singapore, with Singapore at times among the top 10 most polluted cities by air quality.
It has pushed the ratification of a proposed cross-border haze-pollution authority up the agenda, with Indonesia's neighbours keen to take further action.
Firmus is one of many AI companies investing in countries like Singapore. ( Supplied: Firmus )
This summit also comes amid global public uncertainty over the growing capability of artificial intelligence (AI).
The grouping is expected to sign a digital economy framework, something ASEAN says is the first region-wide digital economy agreement.
ASEAN is projected to become the fourth-largest economic bloc by 2030, with a relatively young population, so how it manages future digital transformation could impact the rest of the world.
This year's ASEAN comes right before APEC, where major AI leaders like the US and China will meet.
Some ASEAN countries, like Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, have seen considerable investment in data centres, which have supported their economies during challenging global economic conditions.
"As far as ASEAN is concerned, I think we look positively on (AI)," Ms Lazaro said.
"President Marcos wanted to really emphasise AI in the very first summit in May, but we were sidelined because of the Middle East Crisis."

US President Donald Trump will reportedly use his visit to ASEAN to press South-East Asian countries to join the US-led 'Pax Silica', an initiative that seeks to reduce the reliance on China in the AI supply chain.

items.title: Traditional Aboriginal rock art meets modern style on the world stage
paras: Ivan Namarnyilk paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )

Sitting at a table in a tiny art gallery nestled inside Kakadu National Park, Blaldja artist Ivan Namarnyilk slowly paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass.
But before Namarnyilk even has the chance to finish his pieces, tourists visiting the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre in Jabiru are asking to buy them.
Ivan Namarnyilk says his art is "like the country, the animals, the people, everything has connection". ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
Taught by his father, fellow prominent artist Spider Namirrki, at Mudginberri Station, Namarnyilk has been painting "rock art" on paper since he was a teenager.
More than three decades on, Namarnyilk is keeping his culture alive by passing it on to the next generation.
Known for his detailed, x-ray style works, Namarnyilk mainly uses ochre to paint or scratch-draw local animals and cultural totems before applying his signature, mouth-blown clay handprint.
Ivan Namarnyilk’s art uses natural ochres along with his signature hand print. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
"We use natural colour like red ochre, white clay, yellow ochre," he says.
"I like painting spirit man, kangaroo, echidna, turtle, fish like barramundi or black bream.
"We respect our totems — my father's totem is irritja [wedge-tailed eagle] and my mother's is duwa [mud crab]."
In August, Namarnyilk sold thousands of dollars worth of his art at his first solo exhibition during the Mahbilil Festival in Jabiru.
Ivan Namarnyilk held his first solo exhibition at the Mahbilil Festival in August. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
He says sharing his pieces was "really special" and vital for helping to financially support his family.
Over the past 25 years, more than 500 West Arnhem Indigenous artists have sold pieces at the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre.
Business manager Caron Farrell says the gallery buys artwork "up-front" from about 30 regular makers, with 40 per cent of sales proceeds going towards keeping the centre open.
Caron Farrell says "visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles" on display. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
"This space does all of West Arnhem so it's really important for the artists to be able to bring their art here in all different forms," she says.

items.title: Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat
paras: The Wallabies are running out of time, and excuses. ( AP Photo: Scott Heppell )
It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve, dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm
It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.
But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.
Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".
"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.
Both teams struggled to hold onto the ball in cold and wet conditions. ( Getty Images: David Rogers )

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.
The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of its previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.
But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.
Where the Scots limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.
Scotland barged their way up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.
Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. ( Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol )
The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.
It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.
One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.
One of the most desperate passages came with about quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a line out just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.
A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.
A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.
The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. ( AP Photo: Scott Heppell )
Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.
But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.
Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.
Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.
Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the later was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.
Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.
Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. ( Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol )
Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.
So attention should shift to Wales, who now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).
The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.
But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.
For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.
The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.
They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

items.title: Reserve Bank of India imposes monetary penalty on One Mobikwik Systems Limited
paras: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 06, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹9.00 lakh (Rupees Nine Lakh only) on One Mobikwik Systems Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of the directions issued by RBI on ‘Prepaid Payment lnstruments (PPIs)’ and ‘Fraud reporting’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under the provisions of section 30(1) read with section 26(6) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its operations for the period from June 2025 to March 2026. Based on supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for its failure to comply with the said RBI directions. After considering the company’s reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: the company had allowed fund transfer by certain PPI holders to non-pre-registered beneficiaries beyond the prescribed limit. the company failed to report certain frauds within the prescribed timeline. The action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1496

items.title: Six people arrested in cross-border drugs smuggling network: ED
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network . An investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement ( ED ) unearthed a major drug trafficking operation involving the smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India. Lovejit Singh alias Labba , Manjeet Singh alias Manna were arrested on October 11 while Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh and Ramandeep Singh were arrested on October 18 and one Gurpreet Singh was held on October 20, the agency said in a statement. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons ie Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi. They were were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder.

According to the central probe agency the accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs. According to ED , the investigation under PMLA linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network was initiated based on the seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by DRI and the seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 Kg. of heroin has been seized so far. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where the identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. The accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in the local market. Further, the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles in the second-hand market for trafficking from the storage hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri Madhya Pradesh, and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Previously, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits were attached by the ED . (ANI)

With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture.
